Idea

The meter measures the light on your easel and turns it into a printing time: light × your paper's constant = seconds. Every tool in the device is built on that one number. Once your paper is calibrated, any new light reading becomes a time immediately.

The manual follows the device: first the screen, then the five tabs, then the sidebar, then the jobs that need several steps (calibration, saving, updates).

Words in this manual. A control is something you tap, drag or type into. A readout is a number or message the device shows you. Names printed in bold match the labels on screen. The device is a small screen in a darkroom, so labels are often abbreviated; the full name is given the first time.

Note

The Help button at the bottom of the sidebar opens the Help Center: seven short tabs (Start, Settings, Exposure, Contrast, Split Grade, Virtual Proof and Paper Editor), a QR code to the project page, and the support address shown on the Start tab (support@cyanowood.com). Use it when you are standing at the enlarger and need a reminder.

The Help Center is a quick reminder. This manual is the complete, current reference. If a Help page and this manual disagree, trust this manual.

Tip

The HTML edition (open MANUAL.html in a browser) has a Darkroom button that switches to red-on-black. Use it on a phone or tablet beside the enlarger.

1. Start here

1.1 What the meter does

SafelightIO is a light meter for black-and-white enlarger printing. You put its sensor where the print will be, press Measure LUX, and it tells you how many seconds to expose the paper. It can also:

  • recommend a contrast filter grade from two readings of the negative;
  • work out a split-grade soft + hard exposure;
  • paint a preview grid of the print from a series of readings;
  • check that the enlarger's light is even across the easel.

It is not a densitometer and not a colour analyser. It measures the light that actually falls on the easel, which is what the paper responds to.

1.2 The one thing that makes it accurate

The meter needs one number from you: how sensitive your paper is under your enlarger. You find it once, with one test strip, and type the result into the device. That is paper calibration (chapter 10). After that, every reading becomes a time.

A meter that has not been calibrated for the selected paper cannot give a time. It will show calibrate instead. This is normal, not an error.

1.3 What you need

  • The meter, charged or plugged in.
  • Your enlarger, focused at the height and aperture you will print at.
  • A sheet of the paper you intend to use, for the calibration test strip.
  • A darkroom (or a very dark room) for the sensor's dark calibration.
  • Optional: a microSD card. It keeps settings, papers and sessions on removable storage and makes backups easy.

1.4 Your first session

StepWhat you doWhereTime
1Charge, power on, wait for the main screenUSB-C / power2 min
2Choose Paper Brand, Paper Type and Filter BrandSidebar1 min
3Calibrate the sensor: Calibrate Dark, then Calibrate LightControl Panel tab10 min
4Calibrate the paper with one test stripChapter 1015 min
5Measure the easel and printExposure tab1 min

Steps 3 and 4 are one-time jobs per device/paper. You do not repeat them for every print.

Important

The sensor calibration makes the lux numbers trustworthy. The paper calibration turns lux into seconds. Skipping the sensor step still gives a time, but it may be consistently too long or too short; skipping the paper step gives no time at all.

Step 1 — Power on

Connect USB-C to charge if the battery is low. Press the power button; the splash screen appears with a photography quote, a darkroom tip, the firmware banner (SafelightIO Darkroom Meter v.1.0, Prototype - Not for Sale) and the serial number. After a few seconds the main screen opens.

The backlight is deliberately dim while the device boots, then returns to your saved brightness. If the screen looks almost black, see Brightness in chapter 8 before assuming the meter is broken.

Step 2 — Choose the paper and filter

In the sidebar, set:

  • Filter Brand — the brand of contrast filters in your enlarger (for example Ilford or FOMA). It changes the grade names and the built-in filter factors.
  • Paper Brand and Paper Type — the paper in the easel.

Changing the paper reloads that paper's calibration and trims, and resets the dodge/burn slider. Choose the paper before you measure, not after.

Step 3 — Calibrate the sensor

Open the Control Panel tab and find SENSOR CALIBRATION:

  1. Calibrate Environment Noise → Calibrate Dark, in total darkness.
  2. Calibrate Enlarger Light → Calibrate Light, with the enlarger on and the sensor in steady light.

The full procedure, including the two-phase light calibration, is in section 7.4. Do this once per device; repeat it if readings disagree between gain settings or after a firmware update that changes the sensor settings.

Step 4 — Calibrate the paper

Follow chapter 10. You will make one test strip, choose the correctly exposed midtone, and enter its lux reading and time. The device computes the paper's constant. From then on, the Exposure tab gives times for that paper.

Step 5 — Measure and print

Open Exposure, choose the zone you measured (usually V), press Measure LUX, and read the time. Chapter 3 explains every control on that tab.

2. The screen at a glance

The annotated screen above names the three parts. Each tool chapter opens with its own screenshot, so you can match the labels to the device.

The main screen has three parts:

  • Five tabs across the top: Exposure, Contrast, Split Grade, Virtual Proof, Control Panel. The selected tab is highlighted.
  • The content area in the middle: the controls and readouts for that tab.
  • The sidebar on the right: paper, filter, sensor, calibration values, brightness, battery and the Help button. The sidebar is visible on every tab.

At the bottom of the sidebar the device shows SafelightIO v.1.0. This is the firmware version; it is also on the splash screen and in the Help Center.

Note

The device uses a dim red-on-black screen to protect your night vision. The screenshots in this manual reproduce that look; they can seem darker on paper than the screen does in a darkroom. They were taken before a reading, so values that have no measurement yet show --.

The sidebar is the meter's setup panel. It stays put while you change tabs. The full reference is chapter 8; in short:

  • Battery and Brightness at the top.

Note

The correct spelling is Integration Time. The manual uses the correct spelling in prose and quotes Intergration Time when it refers to the on-screen label, so you can find it on the device.

2.4 Confirmation screens

Some actions cannot be undone, so the device asks first. The screen asks Are you sure? with Yes and No. It is used by:

  • Clear All Calibrations (wipes every paper calibration and the reference);
  • Auto-Est. All Papers (overwrites estimates for uncalibrated papers);
  • Load settings and Load Session (replace current data);
  • Clear under the sensor calibration headings;
  • the second phase of Calibrate Light.

Read the question, then choose. No returns without changing anything.

2.5 The splash screen

At power-on, before the main screen:

  • the banner SafelightIO Darkroom Meter v.1.0;
  • Prototype - Not for Sale;
  • an Inspirational quote and a practical darkroom tip (they change at random); for example Tip: Pre-flash your paper for highlight detail;
  • a closing line such as Have a happy developing sessions!;
  • the serial number and a QR code to the project page.

Nothing on the splash is a control. Wait for the main screen.

3. Exposure

Use this tab when you have a negative and want a printing time.

3.1 The screen

The left column is the measurement: zone, lux reading, calibration constant and the Measure LUX button. The right column is the FILTER & DODGE/BURN panel: filter grade transform, dodge/burn slider, additional time and total time.

The large number at the top is the exposure time. Before you measure it may show a message instead of a number: calibrate, measure lux, no sensor or error. Chapter 13 explains each one.

3.2 Every control and readout

ElementWhat it isWhat to do
EXPOSURE CALCULATORThe tab heading—
Exposure time readoutThe suggested printing time in secondsRead it; it updates after Measure and after filter/dodge changes
SELECT ZONE OF MEASUREMENTOpens the zone listChoose the zone you placed the sensor on; V is the normal midtone
Zone of measurementThe list: 0, I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, XSee the zone table below
LUX READINGThe last measured light level in luxShows the raw measurement
CALIBRATION CONSTANTThe paper's lux × seconds constantSet by paper calibration; read-only here
Measure LUXTakes a reading and calculates the timePress once per measurement; the backlight dims while it reads
FILTER & DODGE/BURNHeading for the right-hand panel—
FILTER GRADE TRANSFORMOpens the filter grade listChoose the filter you will actually use. The grade's factor lengthens the time
DODGE & BURNHeading for the slider and the two times—
Dodge and burn sliderAdds or removes exposure in ¼-stop stepsDrag right to print darker, left to print lighter

TOTAL TIMEBase time + additional timeThis is the time to use at the enlarger
F-StopThe slider's position expressed in f-stopsRead-only; useful when writing notes

3.3 Step by step

  1. Select the paper. In the sidebar choose Paper Brand and Paper Type.
  2. Select the filter. Choose the grade you will put in the enlarger under FILTER GRADE TRANSFORM. “No filter” keeps the time unchanged.
  3. Place the sensor. Put it where the midtone will fall on the easel. Keep your body and the safelight out of the light path.
  4. Choose the zone. V for a midtone; III for a shadow you want to place; VII for a highlight.
  5. Press Measure LUX. Wait for the backlight to return.
  6. Read the time. Use TOTAL TIME if you moved the dodge/burn slider; otherwise use the large exposure time.

3.4 The zone list

The zone tells the meter which tone you measured. A reading at Zone V is the reference. A reading at Zone III is two stops darker, so the meter multiplies the light to find the equivalent Zone V value.

ZoneTone you are measuringMeter factor
0Deep black, almost no detail×32
IBlack with a hint of detail×16
IIDark shadow with texture×8
IIIShadow with good detail×4
IVDark midtone×2
VMiddle gray — the reference×1
VILight midtone÷2
VIIHighlight with texture÷4
VIIIBright highlight, little texture÷8
IXNear white÷16
XPaper white÷32

Tip

Measure V when the sensor sits on the midtone. Measure III when you want to place a shadow, or VII for a highlight. The meter converts either reading to the same exposure scale, so you do not have to move the sensor to a midtone.

3.5 What the filter grade does

A contrast filter absorbs light, so it needs a longer exposure. The meter knows the built-in factor for each grade and brand, and multiplies the base time by that factor. The filter grade also changes the contrast of the print; the meter does not try to compensate for that, because that is the point of the filter.

If you have measured your own filter factor (chapter 12), the device uses your value instead of the built-in one.

3.6 Dodge and burn

The slider is a trim, not a second exposure. It adds or removes time from the whole print in ¼-stop steps, up to ±2.25 stops. Use it when the print is consistently a little light or dark, or when you want to try a variation without recalibrating.

  • ADDITIONAL TIME shows the seconds the slider adds (or subtracts).
  • TOTAL TIME is what you actually expose.
  • The slider resets when you change paper.

For local dodging and burning under the enlarger, use the same total time as your starting point and cover/uncover areas as usual.

3.7 A worked example

A portrait negative, Ilford FP4, printed on Ilford Multigrade Classic Cooltone. The sensor is on the face at Zone VI.

  1. The filter is grade 3, factor about 2.5.
  2. The sensor reads 2.84 lux at Zone VI.
  3. The meter converts Zone VI to the Zone V equivalent: 2.84 ÷ 2 = 1.42 lux.
  4. The paper's constant gives a base time of 8.80 s.
  5. The grade 3 factor makes it 8.80 × 2.5 ≈ 22 s.
  6. The dodge/burn slider at +2 quarter-stops adds about 10 s → ~32 s total.

You do not have to do this arithmetic. The point is that every step has a visible readout, and the TOTAL TIME already includes all of them.

3.8 Common questions

Why does the time change when I change the filter? The filter absorbs light; the factor compensates. The print contrast changes too, which is why you chose the filter.

Why does the time change when I change paper? Each paper has its own calibration and its own trims.

Can I use the meter without calibrating the paper? You can read lux, but you will not get a time. The tab shows calibrate until the paper is calibrated.

The time looks wrong by exactly 2×. Check that you measured the zone you think you did, and that the enlarger height and aperture match the calibration. If they do, run Calibrate Light again.

4. Contrast

Use this tab when you want the meter to recommend a contrast grade.

4.1 What the two readings mean

The meter needs two points in the projected image:

  • HIGHLIGHTS — the dim spot at easel. A highlight on the print comes from a dense part of the negative, so less light reaches the easel.
  • SHADOWS — the bright spot at easel. A shadow on the print comes from a clear part of the negative, so more light reaches the easel.

This is the part that surprises people. Measure the dim part for highlights and the bright part for shadows. The small labels under the headings say exactly that, so you do not have to remember.

4.3 Step by step

  1. Select the paper in the sidebar.
  2. Put the sensor on the dimmest important highlight and press Measure Highlight. Keep your body out of the light.
  3. Put the sensor on the brightest important shadow and press Measure Shadow.
  4. Read CONTRAST RANGE, CONTRAST GRADE and Match Quality.
  5. Put the recommended grade in the enlarger. The Filter Grade readout already includes that grade's exposure factor.
  6. Read EXPOSURE TIME (or Total time if you use the dodge/burn slider).
  7. If the print is consistently off, use the TUNABLES and the Reset button.

Tip

Both readings are required. With one missing, the tab shows -- and the reason is given in the note. Measure the missing point and the result appears immediately.

4.4 How the recommendation works, without the maths

The two readings give a brightness range. A negative with a small range is flat and needs a harder grade; a negative with a large range is contrasty and needs a softer grade. The meter compares the range with the paper's contrast data and picks the closest grade.

  • CONTRAST RANGE is in stops of exposure.
  • CONTRAST GRADE is the recommended filter grade.
  • The time is taken from the middle of the two readings, so the midtone stays put when you change grade.
  • Match Quality tells you how well the negative fits the paper's range.
  • The trims let you move the result without recalibrating.

4.5 Fixed-grade papers

Some papers have one fixed contrast grade. For those papers the tab shows Fixed grade and:

  • the trims are ignored;
  • Split Grade is not applicable;
  • in the Control Panel, the Factor and ISO R fields are disabled; only ISO P can be changed.

The eight fixed-grade papers are listed in chapter 11.2. If you are printing on one, use Exposure and choose the filter grade that matches the paper's grade.

4.6 A worked example

A landscape negative on Ilford Multigrade RC Deluxe:

  • highlight reading 4.10 lux;
  • shadow reading 0.32 lux;
  • the range is about 3.7 stops;
  • the meter recommends grade 1 with Close match;
  • EXPOSURE TIME is 14.2 s.

A grade 1 filter is soft, which suits the contrasty negative. If the print's highlights are too bright, add a small Highlights trim; if the shadows are muddy, add a Shadows trim.

4.7 Common questions

The grade changes when I move one reading slightly. Small changes near a grade boundary can flip the recommendation. Look at Match Quality; Close means either neighbouring grade is reasonable.

The time is not what I expected. The time is for the midpoint, not for the highlight. That is deliberate: it keeps the midtone stable when you change grade.

Should I use Contrast or Split Grade? Use Contrast when one grade suits the whole print. Use Split Grade when the shadows and highlights need different filters.

5. Split Grade

Use this tab when shadows and highlights need different contrast.

5.1 The idea

Split-grade printing gives the print two exposures through two filters:

  • a soft filter for the highlights and midtones;
  • a hard filter for the shadows and blacks.

The meter measures the same two points as the Contrast tab, then works out how much of the total exposure each leg should carry. The result is a pair of times that add up to the print you want.

5.3 Step by step

  1. Select the paper and filter brand.
  2. Measure the dim highlight and the bright shadow, as in chapter 3.
  3. Read the SOFT EXPOSURE and HARD EXPOSURE names and times.
  4. Expose the print: soft leg first, then hard leg (or the reverse, if your workflow prefers; the total light is the same).
  5. If the print needs adjustment, use the trims, then Reset to start again.
  6. Use DODGE & BURN only for a final whole-print shift; it scales both legs.

Warning

The meter may warn that highlights may burn or that contrast is limited. Those warnings mean the requested split is outside what the paper can hold. Choose a less extreme Midtones position, or change the negative.

5.4 How the split is chosen, without the maths

The meter decides what share of the light each leg should carry. At one extreme the print is almost all soft; at the other, almost all hard. The Midtones slider moves that balance. The meter keeps the midtone anchored, so changing the balance does not make the whole print lighter or darker; it changes how the shadows and highlights separate.

The Highlights and Shadows trims adjust the two ends independently. The Exposure and Contrast trims adjust the whole print.

5.5 A worked example

A portrait negative:

  • highlight 8.00 lux;
  • shadow 0.12 lux;
  • the range is about 6.1 stops;
  • the equivalent grade is 00;
  • soft leg: grade 00, 29.5 s;
  • hard leg: grade 5, 6.9 s;
  • total 36.4 s.

The soft leg carries most of the light (about 89%) because the negative is very contrasty. If the highlights are still too dense, add a Highlights trim; if the shadows lose detail, add a Shadows trim.

5.6 Common questions

Why are there two times? The paper receives both exposures. The total is their sum; the split decides where the contrast goes.

Which leg first? It does not matter for the total exposure. Many printers do soft first, then hard; choose one order and keep it for consistency.

The soft and hard filters look odd. The names follow the selected Filter Brand; for FOMA papers a “Special” grade may appear as one of the legs. That is normal.

Can I use Split Grade on a fixed-grade paper? No. The tab will tell you it is not applicable. Use Exposure.

6. Virtual Proof

Use this tab when you want to see how the print will look across the easel before you commit a sheet.

6.1 What it does

The grid divides the easel into cells. You measure each cell; the device paints each cell with the gray it expects on the print at the selected paper and grade. The result is a low-resolution preview of the print, plus a histogram of the tones.

It is a proof, not a scanner: the preview is only as good as the cells you measured.

Enlarger Mode switchTurns the proof into a light-evenness test (section 6.5)Use it with no negative in the carrier
Uniformity LimitThe allowed brightness variation in Enlarger mode, 5–50% (default 15%)Set it to what your printing requires
Stability Detection switchTurns on automatic settling during a scanUse it for hands-free scans
Tolerance (%)How close two reads must be to count as stableSmaller is stricter
Min Stable ReadsHow many stable reads are requiredMore is stricter
Max Wait (ms)The longest the meter waits for a cell to settlePrevents a scan from stalling
Min Delta (lux)A floor for very dim cellsStops noise from looking like change

Note

The four stability fields are used when Stability Detection is on. With it off, each press of Measure records a single reading immediately.

Note

When an automatic scan finishes, the meter picks a provisional Zone V reference: the cell nearest the middle of the measured brightness range in exposure terms. It is a starting point, not a guarantee that the cell is your middle gray. Select the cell you trust and press Set V Zone to take over. A manual, one-cell-at-a-time proof does not set a reference automatically.

6.3 The grid frames

The frame colour tells you what a cell is:

FrameMeaning
AmberThe next cell the meter will read
RedThe cell you selected
CyanThe Zone V reference cell
Light grayHighlight clipping — the cell is too bright for the paper
Dark grayShadow clipping — the cell is too dark for the paper
No frameAn ordinary measured cell

Colour is a shortcut, not the only cue: the selected sample readouts and the histogram tell you the same story in numbers.

6.4 A proof in ten steps

  1. Set Grid Size to a small grid, for example 4 × 3.
  2. Choose the Filter grade you intend to print.
  3. Press Measure for the first cell and place the sensor in the highlighted cell.
  4. Keep pressing Measure (or turn on Stability Detection and let the meter scan) until the grid is filled.
  5. Read the HISTOGRAM. A shape crowded on the right means the print will be bright; crowded on the left means dark.
  6. Tap a cell to see its SELECTED SAMPLE readouts.
  7. If you know the middle gray, select that cell and press Set V Zone.
  8. Change the grade and watch the grid re-render.
  9. Clear Grid to start again; changing Grid Size also clears it.
  10. Save the session if the proof is worth keeping (chapter 9).

Tip

Six cells tell you whether the print is basically even. You do not need a 40 × 30 grid to catch a hot corner or a vignette.

6.5 Enlarger mode — is the light even?

Enlarger mode uses the same grid, but there is no negative in the carrier. The grid becomes a map of the bare enlarger light.

Set up:

  1. Remove the negative. Leave the carrier empty.
  2. Set the lens to the aperture and the head to the height you will print at.
  3. Let the lamp warm up.
  4. Put an opal diffuser over the sensor if you have one; do not let the meter shadow the point you are measuring.
  5. Turn Enlarger Mode on. The filter grade selector is not used in this mode.
  6. Set Grid Size to 3 × 3 (nine points) or 5 × 5 for a finer map.
  7. Press Measure for each point, or turn on Stability Detection and scan.
  8. Select the centre cell and press Set Reference. The centre is the reference for the deviation readouts.

The readouts:

ReadoutMeaning
LuxThe light at the selected point
Dev %How far the point deviates from the reference, in percent
Dev EVThe same deviation in stops
RangeThe spread between the brightest and dimmest points
MeanThe average of all measured points
Min–MaxThe dimmest and brightest points
VerdictGOOD, MARGINAL or UNEVEN

The verdict:

  • GOOD — every point is within half the Uniformity Limit.
  • MARGINAL — the worst point is between half the limit and the full limit.
  • UNEVEN — the worst point is beyond the limit.

The default limit is 15%, which is roughly 0.2 stop. That is a reasonable working tolerance for most enlargers and papers. A stricter limit (for example 10%) is useful for critical work; a looser one (25–30%) may be acceptable for rough proofs.

What the map tells you:

  • dark corners — condenser or diffuser misalignment, or a lens that does not cover the format;
  • a bright centre with dark edges — normal falloff for a condenser enlarger, worse at large magnification;
  • an off-centre hot spot — the lamp is not centred;
  • a single dark cell — something is shadowing that point (your hand, the meter, a cable).

Enlarger mode measurements are kept when you switch back to negative mode, so you can inspect them later. Saving the session stores the mode and the grid (chapter 9).

7. Control Panel

Use this tab to edit filter data, estimate calibrations, save/load, and calibrate the sensor.

The tab is labelled Control Panel. Its main heading is PAPER & FILTER EDITOR. The Help Center calls the same area Paper Editor. The tab has four sections in two columns:

  • PAPER & FILTER EDITOR — left column, top. Override the built-in factors and ISO values.
  • ESTIMATE CALIBRATION — left column, bottom. Copy a calibration to other papers by speed.
  • DATA MANAGER — right column, top. Save and load settings and sessions.
  • SENSOR CALIBRATION — right column, bottom. Dark and light calibration.

7.1 Paper & Filter Editor

This section changes the numbers the meter uses for a paper + filter grade combination. It is for advanced users; the built-in data is good enough for most printing. Edits are saved in flash and survive a power cycle.

ElementWhat it isWhat to do
Select FilterChooses the grade to editPick the grade whose data you want to change
Lengthening FactorThe filter's exposure multiplierRaise it if prints through that filter are too light; lower it if too dark
ISO R RangeThe contrast range this grade producesHigher = softer contrast; lower = harder
Base ISO PThe paper's unfiltered speedHigher = shorter times; lower = longer times. This is per paper, not per grade
FILTER VALUESThe read-only value block—
Factor valueThe effective factor used by every tabShows your override, or the built-in value
Default factor valueThe built-in factory factorReference only
ISO R valueThe effective ISO RShows your override, or the built-in value
Default ISO R valueThe built-in ISO RReference only
ISO P valueThe effective ISO P for the paperShows your override, or the built-in value
Default ISO P valueThe built-in ISO PReference only
ResetClears all overrides for the current paperOther papers keep their overrides
  • A factor of 1.00 means “no exposure change”.
  • A readout shows -- when there is no value to display yet, for example before a grade is selected.
  • Two decimal places are enough for the factor; ISO R and ISO P are whole numbers.
  • The device stores at most 64 overrides. If the list is full, reset a paper you no longer use.
  • On a fixed-grade paper, Factor and ISO R are disabled; only ISO P can be changed.
  • Changing a value commits that field. Selecting another grade commits a pending edit first.

Note

ISO R is the paper's contrast range: a higher number is a softer paper. ISO P is its speed: a higher number means a faster paper and a shorter time. You do not need the standards to use the meter; you only need to know which way the numbers move.

7.2 Estimate Calibration

This section copies a calibration from one paper to another. It is a shortcut for papers you have not calibrated yet; the result is an estimate, not a measurement.

ElementWhat it isWhat to do
ESTIMATE CALIBRATIONThe section heading—
Reference PaperSnapshots the current paper's calibration (lux, time, ISO P)Calibrate one paper well, select it, then press Reference Paper
Reference statusTells you whether a reference is storedIf it says No reference, set one first
Estimate CalibrationEstimates the current paper from the reference, scaled by ISO PUse it for a paper you have not calibrated
Auto-Est. All PapersEstimates every uncalibrated paper from the referenceAsks for confirmation first
Clear All CalibrationsWipes every paper calibration and the referenceAsks for confirmation first; this cannot be undone

The estimate assumes that, at the same light level, a paper with twice the ISO P needs half the time. It is a starting point: make a test strip and adjust.

A sensible workflow:

  1. Calibrate your most-used paper properly (chapter 10).
  2. Select it and press Reference Paper.
  3. Select an uncalibrated paper and press Estimate Calibration.
  4. Print a test strip; if the time is off, calibrate that paper properly or adjust its factor.
  5. Use Auto-Est. All Papers only when you want rough starting points for the whole collection.

7.3 Data Manager

ElementWhat it isWhat to do
DATA MANAGERThe section heading—
Save and Load SettingThe settings group—
Save SettingsWrites the internal flash snapshot and BACKUP.TXTDo it before a firmware update
Load settingsRestores the flash snapshot; rebootsAsks for confirmation first
Save and Load SessionThe session group—
Save SessionWrites the current readings and results to SESSION.CSVUse it to resume later or share a setup
Load SessionRestores a sessionAsks for confirmation if measurements exist
Calibration switch (session load)Include or exclude the stored calibration when loadingOn if you want the session's calibration restored; off to keep the current one
Data manager messageThe result line: saved, loaded, Nothing to export, No session fileRead it if a button seems to do nothing

A session contains the current paper and filter, the last Contrast and Split readings and results, and the Virtual Proof grid (including its mode). It does not contain your whole settings file; use Save Settings for that.

7.4 Sensor Calibration

ElementWhat it isWhat to do
SENSOR CALIBRATIONThe section heading—
Calibrate Environment NoiseThe dark-calibration groupDo it in total darkness
Calibrate DarkMeasures the sensor's electrical noise floorPress once in darkness; it sweeps several settings automatically
Clear (dark)Erases the dark calibrationAsks for confirmation
Sensor calibration statusProgress and result, for example dark calib... 12/24 or dark offsets set (24)Wait for it to finish
Calibrate Enlarger LightThe light-calibration groupDo it with the enlarger on and steady
Calibrate LightMeasures the gain stages against a known light levelFollow the two-phase prompt
Clear (light)Erases the light calibrationAsks for confirmation

Calibrate Dark

  1. Put the sensor in total darkness — cap it, or close the enlarger and turn off all light.
  2. Press Calibrate Dark.
  3. The device sweeps 24 combinations of gain and integration time. It shows dark calib... n/24 while it works; at the slowest settings this takes a few minutes.
  4. Wait for dark offsets set (24). If it says dark calib failed, light reached the sensor; repeat in darkness.

Calibrate Light

  1. Put the sensor in steady enlarger light — no negative, lens open, lamp warmed up. Use a mid-range light level, not the brightest the enlarger can produce.
  2. Press Calibrate Light. The device starts phase 1 and shows gain calib... phase 1/2.
  3. When it asks, dim the light by about four stops (close the aperture or use a neutral density filter) and choose Yes.
  4. Wait for gain cal set. If it says gain cal failed - adjust light, the level was too high or too low; adjust and repeat.
  5. The result is stored. If the light moved during the calibration, it reports - moved; if there was not enough infrared, - no IR; if a stage saturated, - MAX sat or HIGH zero.

Run the light calibration once per device. Repeat it if readings disagree when you switch gain, or after a firmware update that changes the sensor settings.

Important

A safelight, a phone screen or a gap in the enlarger can spoil the dark calibration. A flickering lamp or a moving hand can spoil the light calibration. Both are worth doing carefully once.

8. Settings sidebar

The sidebar is always visible. It holds the choices that affect every tab. From top to bottom the panels hold:

  • battery and Brightness;
  • Filter Brand, Paper Brand and Paper Type;
  • Calibration Lux Value and Calibration Time Value;
  • Sensor Averaging Samples, Sensor Gain and Intergration Time;
  • the battery status line, the version and Help.
ElementWhat it isRange / defaultWhat to do
Battery + barCharge state0–100%See 8.4
Brightness + sliderScreen backlight1–100Set the dimmest level you can read; saves battery and stray light
Filter BrandThe filter system in your enlarger9 brandsChoose the brand printed on your filters
Paper BrandThe paper manufacturerBuilt-in listChoose before measuring
Paper TypeThe paper surface/emulsionBuilt-in listChoose before measuring
Calibration Lux ValueThe lux reading from your calibration test strip0.00–99.99Enter it during paper calibration
Calibration Time ValueThe exposure time that produced the good test strip0.00–99.99Enter it during paper calibration
Sensor Averaging SamplesHow many readings are averaged per measurement1–16, default 5Raise for dim or flickering light; lower for speed
Sensor GainSensitivity stageAuto, LOW, MED, HIGH, MAX; default AutoLeave on Auto unless you need a fixed stage
Intergration TimeHow long each sensor reading lasts100–600 ms, default 200Longer is quieter and slower; shorter is faster
SafelightIO v.1.0Firmware version—Use it when checking an update
HelpOpens the Help Center—Quick reference on the device

8.1 Choosing paper and filter

Paper Brand and Paper Type are linked: choose the brand first, then the paper. Selecting a paper loads its calibration, its trims and its filter data. If you change paper, measure again; the previous readings belonged to the previous paper.

Filter Brand changes the grade names and the built-in factors. It does not change the paper. Choose the brand of the filters you actually own.

8.2 Sensor gain, integration time and samples

These three controls trade speed against noise:

  • Sensor Gain: Auto starts at the most sensitive stage and steps down when the light is bright enough. A fixed stage is useful when you want repeatable readings and you know the light level; if a fixed stage saturates, the reading shows error.
  • Intergration Time: the length of one reading. Longer readings collect more light and are less noisy; shorter readings make a proof scan faster.
  • Sensor Averaging Samples: how many readings are averaged. More samples make a steadier number; fewer make the device feel quicker.

For a Virtual Proof scan, lower the integration time and sample count. For a single critical reading, raise them.

8.3 The calibration values

Calibration Lux Value and Calibration Time Value are the two numbers from your paper calibration test strip. The device divides one by the other to get the paper's constant. You only touch them during calibration (chapter 10).

8.4 Battery, charging and power

The battery bar is red and updates every five seconds. The device has no charger status pin, so it infers charging from the battery voltage:

DisplayMeaning
Discharging + percentageRunning on the battery
Charging... (bar hidden)USB-C connected; the device is charging
Fully chargedThe cell has reached the charger's top voltage
Battery absent (grey, empty)No battery detected; USB-C power only
Battery lowAbout 10% or less; charge now

Notes:

  • Battery low replaces the bar when the charge reaches about 10%. The device has no sleep mode, so the warning stays visible until you charge it.
  • Charging... can stay on after the battery is effectively full, because some chargers stop just below the top voltage the device looks for. This is normal.
  • The bar is voltage-based. Under a heavy load it can sag; a bar that looks empty while the device still runs is not necessarily a dead battery.
  • Charge with USB-C. The battery is protected; unplug when you are done printing.
  • Brightness at 1 is intentionally very dim, not off. Drag right if the screen looks dead.

9. Saving, loading and storage

The meter can keep its data in two places:

  • Internal flash — always present. Settings, calibrations and trims live here.
  • microSD card — optional. It holds copies and files you can move between devices or edit on a computer.
FileWhereWhat it is
SETTINGS.TXTSD cardThe settings file
SETTINGS.BAKSD cardThe previous settings file
PAPERS.CSVSD cardCustom paper definitions
BACKUP.TXTSD cardA readable backup of the settings
SESSION.CSVSD cardOne saved session

9.1 Settings and backups

  • Save Settings writes the internal flash snapshot and BACKUP.TXT. Do this before a firmware update.
  • Load settings restores the snapshot and reboots. It asks for confirmation.
  • Settings changes are flushed about half a second after the last edit. If you cut power immediately after a change, the last change may be lost.
  • With a card inserted, the device also keeps SETTINGS.TXT on the card. On first boot with a card it copies the current settings to the card. If the card is removed, the device falls back to flash.
  • Removing the card is not detected instantly; the sidebar can still say SD: settings.txt until the next save fails. If a save fails, reinsert the card and try again.

9.2 Sessions

A session is a snapshot of the current work, not the whole meter:

  • the selected paper and filter;
  • the last Contrast and Split readings and results;
  • the Virtual Proof grid, its reference and its mode (negative or enlarger);
  • optionally the paper calibration.

Save Session writes SESSION.CSV. Load Session restores it, re-derives the results and asks before overwriting current measurements. The Calibration switch decides whether the session's calibration is restored too.

Sessions are useful when you stop halfway through a print, when you want to compare two negatives, or when you want to send a setup to another meter.

9.3 What is kept, and what is not

  • Settings, paper calibrations, filter overrides and trims live in internal flash.
  • Custom paper definitions live in PAPERS.CSV on the card. Their calibrations are stored on the card too; without the card they are not available after a reboot.
  • BACKUP.TXT is a readable copy, not a second live database.
  • A firmware update preserves the settings record only while the settings format is unchanged. A format change resets the stored settings; the release notes will say so. Recalibrate the sensor and your papers after such an update.

10. Calibrating a paper

Do this once per paper. It is the step that turns lux into seconds.

10.1 Before you start

  • The enlarger is at the height, aperture and lens you will use for real prints.
  • The paper is the one you will print on.
  • The sensor is calibrated (section 7.4).
  • You have a test strip and your usual developer.

10.2 Procedure

  1. Choose the paper in the sidebar.
  2. Set up a normal print. Use a negative with a good midtone and no contrast filter. Focus at the working height.
  3. Place the sensor on the easel where the midtone will fall. Do not let the meter or your hand shadow the point.
  4. Press Measure LUX and write down the lux reading.
  5. Make a test strip at a few seconds, then in steps, through the same lens and aperture. Develop it normally.
  6. Choose the strip with the correct midtone. Note its exposure time.
  7. In the sidebar, enter the lux reading in Calibration Lux Value and the time in Calibration Time Value.
  8. The device computes the constant. Open Exposure and check that it now shows a time instead of calibrate.
  9. Make a full print to confirm. If it is consistently off by a small amount, use the Exposure trim rather than recalibrating.

10.3 What “correct midtone” means

The test strip should show the tone you want for a middle gray — not the lightest strip that still has detail, and not the darkest. The meter uses that point as Zone V. If you choose a different tone, the constant will be biased.

10.4 Redoing a calibration

Repeat the procedure and enter the new lux and time. The new values overwrite the old ones for that paper. You do not need to clear anything first.

Calibrate again if:

  • you change the enlarger, lens or aperture you print at;
  • you change the paper's developer or dilution significantly;
  • the prints are consistently off by a fixed factor and a trim no longer covers it;
  • you replace the sensor.

10.5 Fixed-grade papers

Fixed-grade papers have one contrast grade. The calibration procedure is the same; just use the paper's grade (no variable-contrast filter). The Contrast tab will show Fixed grade and Split Grade is not applicable.

10.6 A calibration checklist

  • ☐ Sensor dark calibration done.
  • ☐ Sensor light calibration done.
  • ☐ Paper selected in the sidebar.
  • ☐ Same lens, aperture and height as real prints.
  • ☐ Sensor on the midtone, not shadowed.
  • ☐ Lux reading written down.
  • ☐ Test strip developed normally.
  • ☐ Correct midtone chosen.
  • ☐ Lux and time entered.
  • ☐ Exposure tab shows a time.

10.7 Worked examples

These examples follow the original guide's test-strip method. The first uses its numbers; the others show common variations.

Example 1 — the first calibration

You are printing on Ilford Multigrade RC Deluxe at f/8, with the head at your usual height and no contrast filter.

  1. You measure 2.50 lux on the midtone.
  2. You make a test strip in 4-second steps: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 s.
  3. The 12-second strip has the middle gray you want.
  4. Enter 2.50 in Calibration Lux Value and 12.0 in Calibration Time Value. The device stores 30.0 lux-seconds (2.50 × 12.0).
  5. With the same negative and no changes, press Measure LUX again. It should read about 2.50 lux, and the Exposure tab should show 12.0 s. That is the check that the calibration is good.

Example 2 — recalibrating after a developer change

You mix a new developer and the same paper now prints darker at the same time.

  1. The light reading is still 2.50 lux.
  2. The test strip says the correct midtone is now 9.0 s, not 12.0 s.
  3. Enter 2.50 and 9.0. The constant becomes 22.5 lux-seconds.
  4. The paper is now calibrated for this developer. The old value is overwritten; there is nothing to clear first.

The constant changed because the paper/developer combination changed. That is expected. If only the enlarger height or aperture changed, the light reading changes instead, and the constant should stay close to the old value.

Example 3 — a fixed-grade paper

You are printing on FOMA FOMASPEED Normal, which has one contrast grade.

  1. Select the paper. Use no contrast filter.
  2. Measure 2.50 lux on the midtone.
  3. The test strip gives 12.0 s. Enter 2.50 and 12.0.
  4. The Exposure tab gives a time. The Contrast tab shows Fixed grade, and Split Grade is not applicable.

The procedure is the same as for a variable-contrast paper. The only difference is that there is no grade to choose.

Example 4 — a second paper from a reference

You have already calibrated Ilford MG FB Classic at 1.42 lux and 8.8 s. You want a starting point for FOMA FOMABROM Variant.

  1. On the calibrated paper, press Reference Paper.
  2. Switch to FOMA FOMABROM Variant.
  3. Press Estimate Calibration.
  4. The meter scales the reference by the paper speed (ISO P 500 → 130), about ×3.85, and suggests 33.9 seconds.

This is a starting point, not a measurement. Make a real test strip before you trust it for critical work.

Example 5 — no strip looks right

The 12-second strip is too dark and the 8-second strip is too light.

  • Make a new strip through the same setup at 9.5, 10.0, 10.5 and 11.0 s.
  • If even the whole strip is too dark or too light, move the range by a full stop and repeat. Do not guess the constant.
  • When one strip is clearly right, enter its time. The constant is what you measured, not what you hoped for.

11. The paper and filter database

11.1 Papers

The built-in database has 22 papers across Ilford and FOMA. Most are variable-contrast; eight are fixed-grade. The Paper Type dropdown is the source of truth for the exact list on your firmware.

Fixed-grade papers:

  • FOMA FOMASPEED Normal
  • FOMA FOMASPEED Hard
  • FOMA FOMABROM Normal
  • FOMA FOMABROM Hard
  • FOMA FOMABROM N chamois, glossy
  • FOMA FOMABROM N chamois, matt
  • FOMA RETROBROM Special, glossy
  • FOMA RETROBROM Special, semi-matt

The variable-contrast papers include the Ilford Multigrade RC and FB families (Deluxe, Portfolio, Warmtone, Cooltone, Classic, ART 300) and the FOMA Variant, Fomabrom Variant, Fomapastel and Fomatone families. Some entries are marked ~ in the database documentation because their values are derived from similar papers rather than measured. They are reasonable starting points; calibrate the paper for critical work.

11.2 Filter brands

The Filter Brand list has nine entries:

BrandGrade names you may see
Ilford00, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
FOMAY, M, and Special variants
AGFA00–5
KODAK00–5
DURST00–5
MEOPTA00–5
BESELER00–5
OMEGA/CHROMEGA00–5
DE VERE00–5

The exact grades offered depend on the paper and the brand. If a grade is not available for the selected paper, it does not appear in the list.

11.3 Adding your own papers

Custom papers are read from PAPERS.CSV on the microSD card at boot. You do not need to rebuild the firmware.

The file has a header line and two kinds of rows:

  • a P row defines a paper (id, manufacturer, type, contrast type, family, Dmin, Dmax, fibre base, ISO P);
  • one or more F rows define that paper's filter grades (grade, factor, ISO R).

Rules:

  • Commas or semicolons separate fields.
  • A P row needs at least 10 fields; an F row needs at least 8.
  • Up to 8 filter rows per paper.
  • A paper whose id matches a built-in replaces it; other ids are added at the end.
  • The file is a template on first boot with a card. Edit a copy, keep the header, and reboot with the card inserted.
  • Calibrations for custom papers live on the card; without the card they are not available after a reboot.

The exact column order is documented in the header comment that the device writes into the template. Keep a backup of the file; it is not part of BACKUP.TXT.

12. Filter factors

12.1 What a filter factor is

A contrast filter absorbs light. The factor is how many times longer the exposure must be to compensate. A factor of 2.0 doubles the time; 1.50 adds half.

The meter has built-in factors for each paper and grade. They are manufacturer averages; your enlarger, lamp and filters can differ by 10–30%. If your prints through a filter are consistently light or dark, adjust the factor in the Control Panel (chapter 7.1).

12.2 Measuring your own factor, simply

  1. Without a filter, make a test strip of a midtone and find the correct time.
  2. With the filter you want to measure, make another strip of the same subject at the same aperture and height.
  3. Divide the filtered time by the unfiltered time. That is the factor.
  4. Enter it in Lengthening Factor for that grade.

Example: 12.0 s unfiltered and 26.4 s filtered → 26.4 ÷ 12.0 = 2.20.

You do not need a densitometer. A consistent test strip is enough.

12.3 Re-measuring

Re-measure after changing the lamp, reflector, lens or filter set; when prints through one grade are consistently off; or once a year if you print often.

12.4 Long exposures

At very long exposures, paper loses some sensitivity (reciprocity failure). The meter applies a correction automatically when the time is long enough, and the Exposure Note tells you when it has done so. You do not need to calculate it. If you override a filter factor, use the measured value; an incorrect factor compounds with the long-exposure correction.

Every print is 2× too light or too darkEnlarger height or aperture differs from calibrationRecalibrate the paper at the height/aperture you print at

Readings disagree when you change gainGain stages uncalibratedRun Calibrate Light
One paper is off, others are fineThat paper's calibrationRecalibrate that paper
Long exposures are offReciprocity correction or a stale filter factorCheck the Exposure Note; remeasure the filter factor

Contrast and Split Grade

SymptomLikely causeFix
-- everywhereA reading is missing or the paper is uncalibratedMeasure both points; calibrate the paper
Grade looks too hard/softMatch Quality is Approximate or a trim is activeCheck the trims; press Reset
Fixed grade shownFixed-grade paper selectedUse Exposure; Split Grade is not applicable
Highlights burn every timeNegative range exceeds the paperChoose a softer grade, or use Split Grade

SymptomLikely causeFix

Every highlight is clippedThe negative is too contrasty for the paper/gradeChoose a softer grade, or use Split Grade
A cell will not settleLight is flickering or the sensor is movingKeep the light steady; raise Max Wait or turn off Stability Detection

Control Panel and data

SymptomLikely causeFix

Reset did nothingReset only affects the current paperSelect the paper you want to reset
Estimate Calibration says No referenceNo reference paperSet Reference Paper first

Screen, power and sensor

SymptomLikely causeFix
Screen looks almost blackBrightness at 1Drag Brightness right
Screen dims during MeasureThe backlight dims to 6% during readsNormal; it restores afterwards
Screen dark for several secondsLong sample count at 600 msReduce samples or integration time
Battery bar empty but device runsVoltage sag under loadCharge; Battery low is the real warning
Charging... never endsCharger stops just below the top voltageNormal
The device does not sleepThere is no sleep modeUse Brightness and charge when needed

Tip

Check the sensor cable, the selected paper, and the battery. The three cause most “wrong reading” reports.

14. Firmware updates

The firmware can be updated over USB-C with a .uf2 file. No special tools or drivers are needed.

14.1 Check your version

The firmware version is v1.0. You can see it:

  • on the splash screen (SafelightIO Darkroom Meter v.1.0);
  • at the bottom of the sidebar (SafelightIO v.1.0);
  • in the Help Center.

14.2 Update

  1. Get the file. Use the firmware file supplied for your meter. The project page is https://atriantas.github.io/SafelightIO/; the QR code on the Help Center's Start tab opens it.
  2. Enter the bootloader. With the meter off, press the small BOOTSEL hole at the top of the device with a pin, keep it pressed, and connect USB-C. The computer shows a removable drive called RP2350.
  3. Copy the .uf2 file to that drive. The meter verifies it and reboots.
  4. Wait for the main screen. Your settings and paper calibrations are kept unless the release changes the settings format.

Warning

Do not install a firmware file for a different device. If the drive does not appear, try a data-capable USB-C cable and press the BOOTSEL hole again.

14.3 If the update does not start

SymptomLikely causeFix
No RP2350 driveThe BOOTSEL hole was not pressed, or the cable is charge-onlyPress the hole with a pin and repeat with a data cable
The file disappears immediatelyThe file is corrupt or for another deviceDownload it again from the project page
The meter still runs the old versionThe copy did not completeRepeat the update
Calibrations are goneThe settings format changedRecalibrate the sensor and your papers

15.2 Glossary

  • Zone — a step on the print's tone scale, from 0 (black) to X (paper white). Zone V is middle gray.
  • Grade — the contrast of the paper/filter combination. Higher grade = harder (more contrast).
  • Stop / EV — a doubling or halving of exposure. One stop = 1 EV.
  • Contrast Range — the brightness range of the negative, in stops.
  • Highlight — the brightest important part of the print; it comes from the dim part of the projected image.
  • Shadow — the darkest important part with detail; it comes from the bright part of the projected image.
  • Midtone — the middle of the tone range; the meter anchors exposure there.
  • Calibration constant — the paper's lux × seconds value. It turns a light reading into a time.
  • ISO R — the paper's contrast range. Higher = softer.
  • ISO P — the paper's speed. Higher = faster, shorter time.
  • Filter factor — how many times longer the exposure is through a filter.
  • Dodge / burn — hold back or add light locally under the enlarger. The device's DODGE & BURN panel is a whole-print trim.
  • Split grade — two exposures through a soft and a hard filter.
  • Virtual proof — a grid preview built from point readings.
  • Uniformity — how evenly the enlarger lights the easel.
  • Reciprocity — the loss of paper sensitivity at very long exposures; the meter corrects for it automatically.
  • Lux — the unit of illuminance the sensor measures.
  • Fixed grade — a paper with one contrast grade; no variable filter.
  • Session — a saved snapshot of the current readings, grid and settings.
  • Reference paper — the calibrated paper used as the source for estimates.

15.4 One-page cheat sheet

I want to…Do this
Get a printing timeExposure → select paper → zone V → Measure LUX → read time
Print a shadow at Zone IIIExposure → zone III → measure the shadow
Choose a gradeContrast → measure highlight (dim) and shadow (bright) → read grade
Split-grade a contrasty negativeSplit Grade → two readings → use soft + hard times
Preview the printVirtual Proof → Grid Size → Measure each cell → read histogram
Check the enlargerVirtual Proof → Enlarger Mode → 3×3 → measure → Set Reference
Calibrate a paperChapter 10: test strip, enter lux and time
Calibrate the sensorControl Panel → Calibrate Dark, then Calibrate Light
Save my workControl Panel → Save Session; Save Settings for a full backup
Update firmwarePress the BOOTSEL hole with a pin, connect USB-C, copy the .uf2 to RP2350
